# Overview

<div style="text-align: justify;">

The **advent of innovative therapies**, particularly in oncology (e.g., immunotherapy), combined with the rapid **rise of artificial intelligence**, has led to a significant increase in the **complexity** of clinical questions and hypotheses. In this context, traditional representation methods (tables, histograms) are no longer sufficient to ensure a high level of analytical performance and presentation quality in the face of these new challenges. It is therefore essential to **innovate in data visualization** by adopting robust, reproducible, and fit-for purpose representations.

We distinguish two main categories of graphics:


<details>
  <summary><strong>Analysis Graphics</strong></summary>
  <p>
    These graphics aim to <strong>enhance the understanding of results</strong>. They allow rapid visualization of population profiles across treatment groups and categorical variables (e.g., sex, HER2 status), help detect statistical differences, and highlight key findings relevant to the clinical trial.
  </p>
  <p><strong>Objectives:</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Facilitate dialogue</strong> among stakeholders involved in the trial</li>
    <li>Provide an <strong>intuitive, fast, and impactful</strong> reading experience</li>
    <li>Serve as a <strong>support for scientific</strong> presentations (articles, conferences, slide decks, posters)</li>
  </ul>
</details>


<details>
  <summary><strong>Patient profile graphics</strong></summary>
  <p>
   These graphics are designed to facilitate and accelerate clinical decision-making.
  </p>
  <p><strong>Objectives:</strong></p>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Visualization</strong> and better <strong>understanding</strong> of the database structure</li>
    <li>Assessment of <strong>data quality</strong> for statistical analysis</li>
    <li>Improved <strong>clinical statistical follow-up</strong> of each patient by highlighting individual and global trends.Through these representations, deriving survival endpoints and longitudinal indicators becomes easier</li>
  </ul>
  <p>
  <strong>Integration in DSMB</strong>: During Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) meetings, these graphics serve as a strategic tool: they enable rapid <strong>detection of inconsistencies</strong>, support timely and <strong>effective decision-making</strong>, and provide critical elements to <strong>ensure patient safety</strong> throughout the study.
  </p>
</details>


These graphics must comply with clinical research standards and are strongly encouraged by international guidelines such as **CDISC, ICH, EMA, and FDA**.

</div>

## Objectives

<div style="text-align: justify;">

The purpose of this work is to **present a set of essential graphical representations** that support the execution of high-quality clinical trials. All examples are derived from datasets structured according to **CDISC** (Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium) standards in **ADaM** (Analysis Data Model) format, ensuring compliance with regulatory and industry requirements. The visualizations are **implemented using R, Python3, and SAS** to demonstrate versatility and adherence to best practices in clinical data analysis.

Data has been generated with [*random.cdisc*](https://insightsengineering.github.io/random.cdisc.data/main/index.html) library of the CRAN in R (Version 4.2.0). Specifically, data used are :
</div>

- **adsl:** Subject-Level Analysis Dataset (ADSL)

- **adae:** Adverse Event Analysis Dataset (ADAE)

- **adrs:** Response Analysis Dataset (ADRS)

- **adlb:** Laboratory Data Analysis Dataset (ADLB)

- **adtte:** Time-to-Event Dataset (ADTTE)

- **adex:** Exposure Analysis Dataset (ADEX)
